extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and students of natural philosophy/evolutionary theory (biologists, sociologists, philosophers)
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and illustrate the general law that any finite homogeneous aggregate—biological, mental, or social—inevitably becomes heterogeneous because its parts are unequally exposed to forces; trace consequences across organisms, minds, societies, and physical bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: The instability of the homogeneous (general law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The instability of the homogeneous: all finite forms of the homogeneous must inevitably lapse into heterogeneity; the relatively homogeneous becomes relatively less homogeneous; the continued changes which characterize Evolution, in so far as they are constituted by the lapse of the homogeneous into the heterogeneous, are necessary consequences of the persistence of force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument illustrated across physical examples (blow on a mass, radiant heat), biological development, mental evolution, language change, and social/industrial differentiation. A priori proof derived from persistence of force: unequal relations of parts to forces produce unlike effects. Only a hypothetical infinite uniform diffusion of identical centres of force could remain stable (not realizable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary differentiation: outside vs inside
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and most general differentiation in organisms is between outer and inner tissues — a contrast answering to the fundamental conditions implied by the terms outside and inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed from protozoa to higher organisms; in unicellular to aggregated cells the peripheral cells coalesce into a membrane (blastoderm) forming an outer layer distinct from interior cells. This follows because surface parts are differently affected by incident forces than interior parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary differentiation of the superficial layer (ectoderm/endoderm)
rubrics_metrics.description: After primary modification (surface vs centre), the superficial portion divides into two layers — the serous and mucous (ectoderm and endoderm) formed respectively from the portions contacting surrounding agents and the contained mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the universal embryonic pattern: peripheral blastoderm becomes two-layered according to differing contacts (external agents vs yolk). Cited as a direct consequence of positional differences of incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation corresponds to differences of position/exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of an organism acquire unlikenesses corresponding to the unlikenesses of their relations to surrounding agencies; e.g. fixed or attitude-preserving organisms develop distinct outer and inner parts and concentric arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sponge (indefinite organization, little differentiation because peripheral/central portions experience similar exposure); Thalamifera (concentric arrangement where outer and inner parts maintain different circumstances). Germs becoming fixed develop specialized upper/lower structures (Marchantia example: rootlets underside, stomata upperside).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental/localized onset of differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiation of surface parts does not occur simultaneously over the whole exterior; it commences at one place and gradually involves the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why peripheral layers form membranes beginning at localized spots and spread (mammals vs birds). This supports expectation that parts exposed unevenly will change first where exposure differs most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species-level heterogeneity from unequal circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: In an assemblage constituting a species, lapse from homogeneity to multiform varieties is caused by members' subjection to unlike sets of circumstances; varieties arise where conditions depart most from the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varieties multiply especially under cultivation/domestication. Natural selection's role is compatible: survival and multiplication of varieties indicate harmony with specific aggregates of surrounding forces; geographical/local differences in aggregates produce local replacement of species by varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental evolution via differential incidence (classification and desynonymization)
rubrics_metrics.description: States of consciousness originally homogeneous become heterogeneous through differences in the changes wrought by different forces; e.g., development of sight leads to ever finer subdivisions (stationary vs moving, near vs remote) and words originally synonymous diverge in meaning (desynonymization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: progressive refinement of visual discrimination as eyes develop; linguistic examples (miscreant, evil-doer vs malefactor, produce, prevent, under/undergo) show unequal usage habits lead to loss of synonymy. Mental changes are framed as nervous functions differing by incidence of forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and governmental differentiation from unequal exposures/interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregates of men, though theoretically uniform in authorities, practically divide into dominant and subordinate parties because of unequal exposure to influences and small initial differences becoming amplified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: business partnerships where one partner tacitly gains authority; boards with emergent dominant directors; political/charitable associations organizing with leaders and masses of uninfluential members. Even an initially absolutely homogeneous group would become heterogeneous due to differences in occupations, conditions, accidents to health, and life experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial specialization due to local material circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic divisions and specializations (agriculture types, mining, ports, manufacture) primarily depend on local differences in soil, climate, resources, and distribution of forces, producing occupations adapted to local functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pastoral vs arable districts, colliers where coal is found, Cornwall mining, Liverpool importing cotton because of proximity to manufacturing districts, Hull for foreign wools. Division of labour interpreted as due to differences in incident forces/distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/physical demonstration from persistence of force
rubrics_metrics.description: An a priori proof: persistence of force implies that like incident forces produce different changes throughout a uniform mass because parts stand in different relations to other forces; unequal quantities/directions of incident force across parts necessarily produce unlike effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical examples: striking a mass (impact compresses contact part and fragments radiate with differing momenta), radiant heat on a sphere (angles and quantities vary across surface), chemical actions affecting surfaces unequally, and mechanical strain distributed unevenly by position. These concretely connect physical law to necessary heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal interactions alone suffice to destroy homogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Even without external incident forces, the unequal actions of parts upon each other (aggregate acting as external force on each minor whole) will work unlike changes in different parts, rendering the whole heterogeneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: treat portions as minor wholes; the aggregate's action on each is an external force, and because these actions differ in amount/direction for different parts, heterogeneity follows. Thus both external and internal forces guarantee instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive and continuing multiplication of effects (ongoing evolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The process is recursive: parts segregate and each part's uniformity is similarly lost, so the lapse into heterogeneity continues — the relatively homogeneous becomes less homogeneous repeatedly, producing continued evolutionary change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusion: the continued changes of Evolution (lapse from homogeneous to heterogeneous and from less to more heterogeneous) are necessary consequences of persistent forces acting at each level; no finite homogeneous form remains stable.
